title: Permissions and Groups
description: Control access to views and models with permissions and user groups.

slides.title: Default Permissions 🛡️
slides.content:
For every model, Django automatically creates three basic permissions:
- `add_modelname` – can add a new instance.
- `change_modelname` – can edit an instance.
- `delete_modelname` – can delete an instance.

These permissions are stored in the `Permission` model and can be assigned to users or groups.

slides.title: Checking Permissions in Views

quizData.question: What are the three default permissions Django creates for a model named `Post`?
quizData.explanation: Django creates add, change, and delete permissions. There is no 'view' permission by default, though it can be added.

slides.title: Using Groups
slides.content:
# Create a group
from django.contrib.auth.models import Group, Permission

editors = Group.objects.create(name='Editors')
permission = Permission.objects.get(codename='change_post')
editors.permissions.add(permission)

# Add user to group
user.groups.add(editors)

# Check if user is in group
if user.groups.filter(name='Editors').exists():
    ...

slides.title: Using `@permission_required` Decorator
slides.content:
Instead of manually checking permissions, you can use the decorator:

```python
from django.contrib.auth.decorators import permission_required

@permission_required('blog.change_post')
def edit_post(request, post_id):
    ...
```

This will redirect unauthenticated users to login, and show a 403 for authenticated users without the permission.

slides.title: Pro Tip 💡
slides.content:
## Use `user.has_perm()` with permission codenames

Permissions are formatted as `app_label.permission_codename`. For example, `blog.change_post`.
